summary: Reviews earlier IAB statements on Internet transparency and discusses new issues. It argues that impeding network transparency, deliberately or not, harms the Internet's ability to support innovation and global communication, and gives illustrations. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 4924 discusses what happens when networks filter, change, or redirect traffic. It explains why those actions can limit new applications and weaken end-to-end security.

questions: why are application layer gateways a problem
why does dns answer rewriting break dnssec
subtitle: The IAB explains how network filtering and rewriting can affect Internet transparency

tldr.problem: Filtering, translation, and redirection in the network can interfere with new applications and change how traffic reaches its destination.
tldr.mechanism: The IAB revisits end-to-end principles and discusses filtering, quality of service, gateways, IPv6 address limits, DNS changes, and load balancing.
tldr.outcome: This Informational statement argues that providers should disclose how services alter traffic and that customer choice matters when applying restrictions.

today: RFC 4924 is an Informational IAB statement published in July 2007. The supplied metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Transparency and End-to-End Communication
sections.content:
A network is transparent, or oblivious to packet content, when it does not filter or transform the data it carries. The IAB argues that this flexibility helps new services work without changes to the network core.

The RFC also recognizes competing goals. Providers may want to block unwanted traffic, while developers and subscribers may value open communication. Because transparency can be difficult to restore after it is lost, the IAB says subscribers should be told how a service handles their traffic.
sections.plainLanguage: A network that leaves traffic unchanged can support new applications without a network upgrade. The IAB says customers should know when a service filters or changes their traffic.

sections.title: Application Filtering and Quality of Service
sections.content:
Filtering applications in the network without customer consent can restrict communication and lead developers to redesign protocols to get around filters. The RFC says filtering at network edges can give customers more control than filtering in the core.

Quality-of-service rules can also affect whether applications work. Some traffic classes may experience more packet loss, and application-specific bandwidth limits can have the same effect as blocking an application. The RFC recognizes that customers may choose limits for their own networks.
sections.plainLanguage: Network filters can block applications or push developers to work around them. Traffic priorities and limits can also make an application unusable, so providers should explain these restrictions.

sections.title: Gateways, IPv6 Addresses, and DNS Changes
sections.content:
Application-layer gateways may need updates when a new address-dependent application appears. The RFC argues that this dependency is part of how gateways work, not only a problem with poor implementations.

Limiting IPv6 address allocation can encourage network address translation, which the IAB considers a barrier to transparency. The RFC also warns that rewriting DNS answers between authoritative servers and client resolvers can cause DNSSEC validation to fail.
sections.plainLanguage: A gateway may need special rules for each application it handles. Changing DNS answers in transit can also stop DNSSEC, which checks whether DNS data was altered.

sections.title: Load Balancing and Redirection
sections.content:
Load balancing and redirection can send requests to different servers based on the apparent location of a request. The RFC notes that these techniques can be useful when implemented well, but can also direct users to a server that is not near them or interrupt service.

For example, DNS redirection may use the address of a distant DNS server rather than the requesting host. Misconfigured packet filters can also send traffic onto an overlay path that delays or drops it, while anycast requires planning for routing changes.
sections.plainLanguage: Redirecting traffic can improve service, but it can also send a user to the wrong server. DNS redirection may reflect the location of the DNS server rather than the user.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC says network address translation, transparent proxies, and DNS namespace changes can weaken end-to-end security and interfere with protocols designed to strengthen it. A security boundary may also leave internal systems exposed if an attacker gets past it.

The IAB notes that restrictions may still be needed, but says applying them at the network edge can offer more flexibility than applying them throughout the network.
sections.plainLanguage: Changing traffic in the network can interfere with security checks between endpoints. The RFC favors giving customers clear information and control over restrictions where possible.
